name: African Lion
habitat: Grassland, savanna, and open woodland across Sub-Saharan Africa, with a single remnant population in India's Gir Forest.
dietText: Hunts in coordinated prides — wildebeest, zebra, and buffalo are primary prey.
facts: A pride's roar can be heard from 8 km away.
Lionesses do 85–90% of the pride's hunting.
Males can sleep up to 20 hours a day.
conservation: Population has declined by ~43% since the early 1990s due to habitat loss and human conflict.

name: Snow Leopard
habitat: High-altitude alpine zones of Central and South Asia, 3,000–4,500 m elevation.
dietText: Preys on blue sheep, ibex, and marmots across steep mountain terrain.
facts: Cannot roar — makes a distinctive chuff-like call.
Tail can equal body length, used for balance.
Leaps up to 15 metres in a single bound.
conservation: Fewer than 10,000 mature individuals remain, threatened by poaching and habitat fragmentation.

name: Blue Morpho Butterfly
habitat: Lowland tropical rainforest across Central and South America.
dietText: Adults sip fermenting fruit juice and tree sap; caterpillars feed on legumes.
facts: Iridescent blue comes from scale structure, not pigment.
Underwings are dull for camouflage at rest.
Flash-and-vanish flight confuses predators.
conservation: Locally abundant, though deforestation threatens habitat in parts of its range.

name: Red Fox
habitat: Forests, grasslands, mountains, and increasingly urban edges across the Northern Hemisphere.
dietText: Opportunistic — small mammals, birds, insects, fruit, and human food scraps.
facts: Can hear a watch ticking 40 m away.
Uses Earth's magnetic field to judge pounces.
Has over 40 distinct vocalisations.
conservation: Population stable and expanding into urban habitats worldwide.

name: White-tailed Deer
habitat: Forest edges, meadows, and farmland across the Americas.
dietText: Browses leaves, twigs, fruit, nuts, and agricultural crops seasonally.
facts: Raises its tail as a white flag to warn the herd.
Fawns are scent-free at birth.
Antlers regrow annually.
conservation: Abundant across most of its range, with populations exceeding historic norms in places.

name: Great Horned Owl
habitat: Forests, deserts, wetlands, and suburban parks across the Americas.
dietText: Apex nocturnal hunter — rabbits, skunks, and other raptors.
facts: Grip severs a rabbit's spine instantly.
Rotates its head up to 270°.
"Horns" are feather tufts, not ears.
conservation: Stable populations, benefiting from adaptability to altered landscapes.

name: Green Sea Turtle
habitat: Tropical and subtropical coastlines, seagrass beds, and coral reefs worldwide.
dietText: Adults graze almost exclusively on seagrass and algae.
facts: Can hold its breath for up to 5 hours while resting.
Returns to its natal beach to nest.
Named for the green fat beneath its shell, not its colour.
conservation: Endangered from bycatch, coastal development, and historic overharvesting of eggs.

name: Humpback Whale
habitat: All major oceans — feeds in polar waters, breeds and calves in tropical waters.
dietText: Filters krill and small schooling fish using baleen plates, often via bubble-net hunting.
facts: Songs can travel across entire ocean basins.
Migrates up to 8,000 km annually — one of the longest of any mammal.
Pectoral fins can reach 5 m — the longest appendage of any animal.
conservation: Recovered significantly since the 1986 whaling moratorium; some subpopulations remain at risk.

name: American Bison
habitat: Prairie grasslands and river valleys of North America.
dietText: Grazes almost exclusively on native grasses and sedges.
facts: Can sprint up to 55 km/h despite its bulk.
Wallows in dust to deter insects and shed fur.
Once numbered over 30 million before near-extinction in the 1800s.
conservation: Recovered from fewer than 1,000 individuals through conservation herds, though wild-ranging populations remain limited.

name: Poison Dart Frog
habitat: Humid lowland rainforest floors of South America.
dietText: Feeds on ants, termites, and small invertebrates that contribute to its toxicity.
facts: Toxicity comes from its diet — captive-bred frogs aren't poisonous.
Bright colouring warns predators: a textbook case of aposematism.
Some species carry tadpoles on their backs to individual water pools.
conservation: Stable in protected rainforest, though habitat loss threatens regional populations.

name: Clownfish
habitat: Coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific, always paired with a host sea anemone.
dietText: Eats algae, zooplankton, and anemone leftovers in a mutualistic relationship.
facts: A mucus coating makes it immune to anemone stings.
All clownfish are born male; the dominant fish in a group becomes female.
Rarely strays more than a few metres from its host anemone.
conservation: Stable in the wild, though reef degradation and the aquarium trade are regional pressures.
